items.stem: A nurse realises an entry made two hours ago recorded the wrong medication dose. What is the correct way to fix the record?

options.text: Add a dated, signed correction that marks the original as an error while keeping it visible
options.rationale: Correct: the record is a legal document; errors are amended with a tracked, dated and signed correction, not erased.

options.text: Delete the original entry and type the right dose in its place
options.rationale: Overwriting destroys the audit trail and can appear as concealment.

options.text: Use correction fluid or black out the line on the printout
options.rationale: Obscuring the original removes evidence of what was recorded and when.

options.text: Leave it unchanged because the next clinician will notice
options.rationale: Leaving a known error uncorrected risks patient harm and misrepresents care.

items.explanation: Correct: the record is a legal document; errors are amended with a tracked, dated and signed correction, not erased.

items.stem: Which TWO features make a clinical note higher quality? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It records the clinical reasoning behind the assessment and plan
options.rationale: Correct: documented reasoning lets other clinicians follow and safely continue care.

options.text: It is completed close to the time of the encounter
options.rationale: Correct: timely entries are more accurate and support continuity.

options.text: It is as long as possible to show thoroughness
options.rationale: Length is not quality; note bloat hides the clinically relevant detail.

options.text: It copies the previous visit's note forward unchanged
options.rationale: Unedited copy-forward content misrepresents the current encounter.

items.explanation: Correct: documented reasoning lets other clinicians follow and safely continue care.
items.domain_ref: Quality and clinical reasoning in notes

items.stem: In a SOAP note, a patient's reported symptoms described in their own words belong in which section?

options.rationale: Correct: the Subjective section captures what the patient reports, including symptoms in their own words.
Objective holds measurable findings such as vital signs and exam results, not patient-reported symptoms.
Assessment records the clinician's interpretation and diagnosis, not the raw report.
Plan documents next steps such as tests and treatment, not the patient's report.

items.explanation: Correct: the Subjective section captures what the patient reports, including symptoms in their own words.
